aeo.what_is: Intense preoccupation with perceived appearance flaws that causes distress and repetitive behaviors like mirror-checking or excessive grooming.

description.overview: A preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others. Individuals perform repetitive behaviors or mental acts in response to these concerns, causing significant distress or impairment.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: Spending 3 hours before work applying makeup to cover a 'crooked nose' that others don't notice
Checking mirrors 50+ times daily while convinced your skin looks 'diseased'
Refusing to leave the house without a hat because your hairline is 'receding terribly'
Canceling dates repeatedly because you're certain your jaw is 'asymmetrical and deformed'
Working out 5 hours daily while believing you're 'scrawny' despite visible muscle mass
Avoiding all photos and social media because you think you look 'hideous'
Seeking multiple cosmetic procedures but feeling worse after each one
Missing work regularly because grooming rituals take hours to complete
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief that their suffering has a name and isn't 'just vanity'
Skepticism because they're convinced the flaw is real and visible
Shame about the extent of time spent on appearance concerns
Fear that treatment means accepting an 'ugly' appearance
Confusion about how others don't see what seems so obvious
Hope that therapy might reduce the constant distress
Resistance if insight is poor or absent (delusional beliefs)

content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects/flaws in appearance not observable or slight to others. B. At some point, performance of repetitive behaviors (mirror checking, excessive grooming, skin picking, reassurance seeking) or mental acts (comparing appearance to others) in response. C. Clinically significant distress or impairment. D. Appearance preoccupation not better explained by concerns with body fat/weight in an eating disorder.

temporal_criteria.duration: No specific minimum duration required, but preoccupation must be persistent and associated with repetitive behaviors or mental acts.
temporal_criteria.pattern: Typically chronic and fluctuating; severity may increase during stress or life transitions.
temporal_criteria.onset_considerations: Usually emerges in adolescence; gradual onset with increasing time spent on appearance concerns and rituals.

content.prevalence: Approximately 2% in the general population; higher rates in dermatology, cosmetic surgery, and orthodontic settings.
content.age_of_onset: Typically emerges in adolescence, coinciding with increased self-consciousness about appearance.
content.prognosis: Often chronic without treatment. Early intervention with psychotherapy and/or medication improves outcomes.

circuitry: Hyperactivity in the frontostriatal and occipitotemporal networks, especially the left hemisphere visual processing regions, leading to detail-focused processing.
Abnormalities in amygdala and anterior cingulate activation linked to heightened emotional salience of perceived defects.
neurochemistry: Possible dysregulation in serotonin pathways, similar to OCD; some evidence for dopaminergic involvement.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Family history of OCD or anxiety disorders; early teasing, abuse, or cultural pressures regarding appearance increase vulnerability.

history_psychosocial: Onset and course of appearance concerns; specific body areas involved.
Time spent daily on preoccupation and related behaviors.
History of cosmetic procedures and satisfaction with results.
Suicidality, self-harm history, comorbid psychiatric conditions.
medical_assessment: Physical exam to rule out true anomalies.
Dermatologic or dental evaluation only when clinically indicated.
Avoid unnecessary cosmetic referrals without psychiatric screening.
standardized_measures: BDD-YBOCS (Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale modified for BDD).
risk_stratification: Assess for suicidal ideation or attempts (high rates in BDD).
Evaluate for social isolation, severe depression, or aggression toward perceived defect.
Identify history of poor outcomes from cosmetic procedures.
differential_diagnosis: OCD with contamination or symmetry themes.
evaluation.team_and_process: Coordinate with psychiatry, psychology, and primary care; educate non-psychiatric providers on risks of cosmetic intervention in untreated BDD.

core: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts in response
Distress or impairment related to appearance concerns
associated_features: Seeking reassurance or comparing with others

severity_levels.mild: Preoccupation present but manageable; repetitive behaviors under 1 hour/day.
severity_levels.severe: Preoccupation over 3–8 hours/day; severe avoidance and inability to function.

biological: Family history of OCD, BDD, or anxiety
Neurobiological abnormalities in visual and emotional processing circuits
environmental: Occupations or activities focused on looks

impact_on_life.school_work: Absenteeism, lateness due to grooming rituals; decreased performance.
impact_on_life.social: Avoidance of events; strained relationships; isolation.
impact_on_life.medical: Multiple unnecessary cosmetic procedures with poor satisfaction.
impact_on_life.emotional: High anxiety, depression, shame; increased suicide risk.

psychotherapy: CBT tailored for BDD with exposure and response prevention.
medications: SSRIs (fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, sertraline, escitalopram) at higher OCD-range doses.
Augmentation with atypical antipsychotics (e.g., risperidone) if delusional intensity persists.
lifestyle_interventions: Reduce mirror-checking and avoidance through graded exposure.
care_coordination: Educate dermatologists/plastic surgeons to screen for BDD.
Collaborate with family/support network for adherence and monitoring.

treatment_goals: Prevent relapse and reduce suicide risk.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Attributing distress solely to low self-esteem or depression without assessing appearance preoccupation.
Misinterpreting as vanity or normal adolescent concern.
Overlooking in males, where BDD may focus on muscle size (muscle dysmorphia).
overdiagnosis_factors: Labeling normal appearance dissatisfaction as BDD without significant distress or impairment.
Confusing with culturally normative grooming or fitness focus.
Misdiagnosing eating disorders as BDD when weight/shape is the primary concern.

commonly_confused_with.why_confused: Both involve obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviors; similar neural pathways and response to SSRIs.
commonly_confused_with.key_differences: In BDD, obsessions are specifically about appearance; in OCD, themes vary (contamination, harm, symmetry). BDD involves perceptual distortions of physical features.

commonly_confused_with.why_confused: Body image distortion and preoccupation with appearance are present in both; both involve repetitive behaviors.
commonly_confused_with.key_differences: Eating disorders focus primarily on weight and body fat/shape; BDD concerns other features (nose, skin, hair, muscle definition). Eating disorders involve specific eating/purging behaviors.

commonly_confused_with.why_confused: Both involve fear of negative evaluation and social avoidance; anxiety in social situations is prominent.
commonly_confused_with.key_differences: Social anxiety stems from fear of judgment about behavior/performance; BDD stems from conviction about specific appearance defects. BDD includes repetitive checking/grooming behaviors not typical of social anxiety.

commonly_confused_with.why_confused: When insight is absent in BDD, beliefs about appearance can be delusional in intensity; both involve fixed false beliefs.
commonly_confused_with.key_differences: BDD is diagnosed even when beliefs are delusional, if they're specifically about appearance and accompanied by characteristic repetitive behaviors. BDD responds to SSRIs and CBT, while delusional disorder typically doesn't.

clinical_pearls: Ask specifically about time spent on appearance concerns and mirror use—routine questions about 'body image' may miss BDD.
If someone seeks cosmetic procedures repeatedly or is dissatisfied afterward, screen for BDD before referral.
Muscle dysmorphia in males is often missed—ask about excessive exercise, steroid use, and beliefs about being 'too small.'
Poor insight doesn't mean psychosis—BDD can include delusional conviction but still responds to BDD-specific treatment.

first_person_statements: I know people say they don't see it, but when I look in the mirror, my nose is obviously huge and crooked. I can't understand how they're all lying to make me feel better.
I've had three nose jobs and I still hate my face. Each surgeon says it looks great, but I know they're just trying to get paid. I'm saving for another one.
I spend so long getting ready that I'm late to everything. My friends stopped inviting me out. They think I'm flaky, but I just can't leave until I look okay.
The gym is the only place I feel sort of okay because at least I'm doing something about how scrawny I look. But even after two years of lifting, I still look tiny.
I deleted all my social media because I couldn't stand seeing photos of myself. Every picture confirmed how ugly I am compared to everyone else.
My therapist keeps saying my skin looks fine, but I can see every pore, every uneven texture. I've spent thousands on dermatologists and nothing helps.

insight: Good/fair insight: recognizes beliefs are probably not true
Poor insight: thinks beliefs are probably true
Absent insight/delusional beliefs: completely convinced beliefs are true
specifiers.muscle_dysmorphia: Preoccupation with idea that body build is too small or insufficiently muscular

self_help_strategies: Limit mirror use to functional purposes only.
Engage in activities unrelated to looks.

childhood: May present as reluctance to be photographed or avoidance of certain activities; excessive concern with a minor feature.
adolescence: Increased self-consciousness; long grooming times; school avoidance; possible onset of muscle dysmorphia in males.
adulthood: Occupational and relationship difficulties; chronic dissatisfaction despite procedures.

real_life_examples.title: The Mirror Trap
real_life_examples.story: Marcus, 19, started college excited to make new friends. But within weeks, he became convinced his ears stuck out 'like an elephant.' He began checking his reflection in every window, phone screen, and mirror he passed—sometimes 60 times a day. He bought hats to cover his ears and turned down invitations to parties, certain people were staring and judging. His roommate noticed Marcus spent hours positioning his hair to hide his ears and asked if he was okay. Marcus showed him photos, asking 'Can't you see how deformed they are?' His roommate saw completely normal ears. Marcus started skipping classes, too anxious to be seen. He researched plastic surgeons and spent his food money on consultations, but each surgeon said his ears were proportional and didn't need surgery.

real_life_examples.title: Never Enough Muscle
real_life_examples.story: Tyler, 24, worked out religiously for three years, building significant muscle mass that friends admired. But when he looked in the mirror, he saw a 'scrawny, weak body.' He started going to the gym twice a day, spending four hours total, and began researching steroids. His girlfriend expressed concern about his obsession, but he insisted he was 'just trying to not look pathetic.' At the beach, he wore a shirt, convinced his arms were 'twigs' compared to other men. He declined social events if they conflicted with gym time, and his relationship suffered. Co-workers commented on his physique positively, but Tyler interpreted this as pity or sarcasm. He took dozens of selfies daily, analyzing muscle definition and feeling increasingly disgusted.

real_life_examples.title: The Skin She Couldn't Fix
real_life_examples.story: Aisha, 27, became fixated on her facial skin texture after a friend casually mentioned 'large pores.' She began examining her face under magnifying mirrors for hours, convinced her skin looked 'diseased and crater-filled.' She visited five dermatologists in six months, demanding treatments for skin they all said looked healthy. She spent thousands on facials, lasers, and chemical peels, but felt worse after each one. She stopped going to work happy hours, certain colleagues were repulsed by her skin. Her morning routine expanded to two hours of makeup application, layering products to achieve 'perfect smoothness.' When she arrived late to work repeatedly, she was placed on a performance improvement plan. Friends tried to reassure her, but she believed they were being polite. She researched radical treatments abroad.

real_life_examples.title: The Asymmetry Obsession
real_life_examples.story: Jordan, 31, became convinced one side of his face was 'collapsing' and asymmetrical. He spent work meetings positioned so colleagues only saw his 'good side' and avoided video calls entirely. He took hundreds of photos weekly, measuring facial features with apps and comparing minute differences. His partner grew frustrated with constant requests for reassurance—'Does my face look crooked?'—which Jordan asked dozens of times daily. He consulted three plastic surgeons about facial implants or procedures to 'even out' his face; all declined, saying his face was normally symmetrical. Jordan interpreted their refusals as evidence that his case was too severe to fix. He began researching surgeons in other countries and maxed out a credit card on consultations.

real_life_examples.title: The Hairline That Wasn't
real_life_examples.story: Priya, 23, became convinced her hairline was receding and making her look 'old and ugly' despite having a full head of hair. She combed through online forums about hair loss, interpreting every shed hair as catastrophic. She stopped wearing ponytails, convinced they revealed 'bald patches,' and spent an hour each morning styling her hair to cover her forehead. She avoided wind and water, afraid her hair would move and expose her 'deformity.' Dating felt impossible—she canceled three first dates at the last minute, panicking about her appearance. She tried minoxidil, supplements, and scalp treatments despite her doctor saying she showed no hair loss. Her search history filled with hair transplant clinics, and she began saving aggressively for a procedure she believed would finally make her 'normal.'

comparisons.similarities: Both involve noticing and occasionally disliking aspects of one's appearance; both may include grooming or makeup use.
comparisons.differences: BDD involves distressing preoccupation (1+ hours daily), repetitive behaviors that are difficult to control, and significant functional impairment. Normal concerns are fleeting and don't severely impact life.
comparisons.clinical_significance: The key distinction is intensity, time consumed, level of conviction, and degree of impairment.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve fear of negative evaluation and avoidance of social situations; both cause significant distress.
comparisons.differences: Social anxiety centers on fear of judgment about behavior or performance; BDD centers on specific perceived appearance defects. BDD includes repetitive checking, grooming, or reassurance-seeking not typical in social anxiety.
comparisons.clinical_significance: Ask what the person fears others will notice—specific appearance flaws suggest BDD; general embarrassment or saying something wrong suggests social anxiety.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve distorted body image, preoccupation with appearance, and behaviors aimed at 'fixing' perceived flaws; both can be severe and life-threatening.
comparisons.differences: Anorexia focuses on weight and body fat/shape with restrictive eating and fear of weight gain; BDD focuses on other features (skin, nose, hair, muscle) without eating restriction as the primary behavior.
comparisons.clinical_significance: If preoccupation is exclusively about weight/shape and involves restrictive eating or purging, diagnose eating disorder. BDD can co-occur with eating disorders.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve intrusive, distressing thoughts and compulsive behaviors to reduce anxiety; both respond to SSRIs and ERP therapy.
comparisons.differences: OCD obsessions cover diverse themes (contamination, harm, order); BDD obsessions are exclusively about appearance. BDD involves perceptual distortions (actually seeing defects that aren't there).
comparisons.clinical_significance: BDD is in the OCD-related category but requires specific appearance focus. Can co-occur with OCD.

faqs.question: Is BDD just vanity or caring too much about looks?
faqs.answer: No. BDD is a serious mental health condition involving distressing, intrusive thoughts about appearance that consume hours daily and cause significant impairment. People with BDD aren't vain—they're suffering from perceptual and cognitive distortions they can't control.

faqs.question: Can you have BDD even if other people see the flaw you're concerned about?
faqs.answer: BDD involves preoccupation with perceived defects that are 'not observable or appear slight to others.' If a noticeable feature exists but the preoccupation is excessive and out of proportion, BDD may still apply. The key is the severity of distress and impairment relative to the actual appearance.

faqs.question: Will cosmetic surgery help someone with BDD?
faqs.answer: Typically no. Research shows most people with BDD remain dissatisfied after cosmetic procedures, often focusing on the same area or shifting to a new perceived flaw. Surgery doesn't address the underlying perceptual and cognitive distortions. Treatment should focus on therapy and medication.

faqs.question: What's the difference between BDD and muscle dysmorphia?
faqs.answer: Muscle dysmorphia is a specifier of BDD where the preoccupation is with being too small or not muscular enough, despite often having above-average muscle mass. It's more common in males and involves excessive exercise, strict diets, and sometimes steroid use.

faqs.question: How is BDD different from an eating disorder?
faqs.answer: Eating disorders primarily involve preoccupation with weight and body fat/shape, with behaviors like restricting food, bingeing, or purging. BDD focuses on other appearance features (skin, nose, hair, symmetry) without eating/weight as the primary concern. Both can co-occur.

faqs.question: Can children have BDD?
faqs.answer: Yes, though it most commonly begins in adolescence. Children may show excessive concern about a specific feature, avoid photos or mirrors, seek constant reassurance, or refuse activities due to appearance worries. Early intervention is important.

faqs.question: What does 'poor insight' or 'delusional' BDD mean?
faqs.answer: Some people with BDD are completely convinced their perceived defect is real and obvious to others (delusional intensity). This doesn't change the diagnosis to a psychotic disorder—it's still BDD, but the 'absent insight/delusional' specifier is added. Treatment is similar.

faqs.question: Is BDD more common in people who work in appearance-focused fields?
faqs.answer: BDD affects people across all professions, but prevalence may be higher in settings like modeling, acting, or fitness industries where appearance scrutiny is intense. However, BDD is a clinical disorder, not a normal byproduct of those careers.

faqs.question: How much time does someone with BDD spend on appearance concerns?
faqs.answer: People with BDD typically spend at least an hour per day preoccupied with their perceived flaws. Many spend 3-8+ hours daily on mirror-checking, grooming, camouflaging, reassurance-seeking, or researching fixes. This time consumption severely impacts functioning.

faqs.question: Can BDD go away on its own?
faqs.answer: BDD is often chronic without treatment. While symptoms may fluctuate, they rarely resolve spontaneously. Evidence-based treatment (CBT and/or SSRIs) significantly improves outcomes, and early intervention leads to better prognosis.

faqs.question: What's the suicide risk with BDD?
faqs.answer: BDD has one of the highest suicide rates among mental health conditions, with studies showing lifetime suicide attempt rates of 20-30%. The combination of severe distress, shame, and hopelessness makes assessment and treatment urgent.

faqs.question: How is BDD treated?
faqs.answer: First-line treatments are CBT tailored for BDD (including exposure and response prevention) and SSRIs at higher doses (similar to OCD treatment). Combination therapy is often most effective. Cosmetic procedures are not recommended as primary treatment.

faqs.question: Can medication alone treat BDD?
faqs.answer: SSRIs can significantly reduce symptoms, but combining medication with BDD-specific CBT typically produces better and more durable results. Therapy helps address perceptual distortions, reduce rituals, and build coping skills that medication alone doesn't provide.

faqs.question: What should I do if someone I love refuses to believe they have BDD?
faqs.answer: Poor insight is common in BDD. Avoid arguing about whether the flaw is real. Instead, focus on the distress and impairment: 'I can see this is causing you a lot of pain and affecting your life. Would you be willing to talk to someone about the distress, even if we disagree about the appearance issue?'

faqs.question: Is mirror-checking always a sign of BDD?
faqs.answer: No. Occasional mirror use is normal. BDD involves excessive checking (often dozens to hundreds of times daily) or complete mirror avoidance, driven by distressing preoccupation. The frequency, distress, and impairment distinguish BDD from normal grooming.

faqs.question: Can BDD affect any body part?
faqs.answer: Yes. Common areas include skin, hair, nose, teeth, weight/body shape, and muscle size/definition, but BDD can focus on any perceived defect. Some people are preoccupied with multiple areas simultaneously.

faqs.question: How long does treatment for BDD take?
faqs.answer: CBT for BDD typically involves 12-24 weekly sessions, though some people need longer. SSRIs require 10-12 weeks at adequate doses to see full benefit. Many people continue treatment for months to years to maintain gains and prevent relapse.

faqs.question: What's the difference between BDD and just wanting to look better?
faqs.answer: Wanting to look better is universal. BDD involves distressing, intrusive preoccupation (not just preference), time-consuming repetitive behaviors, perceptual distortions (seeing defects others don't), and significant functional impairment. The distress and impairment are key.

faqs.question: Can social media make BDD worse?
faqs.answer: Social media can exacerbate BDD by providing constant appearance comparisons, filtered images that distort reality, and reinforcement of appearance focus. Many people with BDD avoid social media entirely or engage in excessive comparison and reassurance-seeking online.

faqs.question: Is BDD related to OCD?
faqs.answer: Yes. BDD is classified in the DSM-5 as an obsessive-compulsive and related disorder. Both involve intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviors, share neural pathways, and respond to similar treatments (SSRIs and ERP). However, BDD has unique features like perceptual distortion.

content.when_to_seek_help: Seek professional help if preoccupation with appearance consumes more than an hour/day, causes distress or impairment, or if suicidal thoughts emerge.

challenging_factors: High comorbidity with depression or OCD
